title: Ai Falls and the Law Is Read
overview: After an earlier defeat, Israel takes the city of Ai by ambush and destroys it, then gathers at two mountains to renew its covenant (its binding agreement) with the LORD by hearing the law of Moses read aloud.

parts.label: A second try at Ai (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: After a defeat caused by one man secretly taking forbidden goods, the LORD tells a shaken Joshua to try again with the whole army. This time, unlike at Jericho, the people may keep the animals and goods they capture.

parts.label: Setting the trap (vv. 3-13)
parts.note: Joshua hides troops west of Ai, toward the town of Bethel, while the main army camps in plain sight to the north. The text gives both 30,000 and 5,000 for the hidden force, and interpreters are unsure whether these are two groups or one.

parts.label: The fake retreat (vv. 14-23)
parts.note: Israel pretends to run away and draws every defender out, and when Joshua raises his javelin as a signal, the hidden troops take Ai and set it on fire. Seeing the smoke, the army turns back and traps the men of Ai between two forces, taking only their king alive.

parts.label: Ai wiped out (vv. 24-29)
parts.note: The text says all 12,000 people of Ai, men and women, were killed and the city left a ruin, though archaeologists debate how this fits what the site shows. The king's body was hung on a pole as a public warning, then taken down at sunset as the law of Moses required and buried under a pile of stones.

parts.label: An altar on Mount Ebal (vv. 30-32)
parts.note: Near the town of Shechem, about twenty miles north, Joshua builds the altar Moses had called for, made of rough stones untouched by iron tools, and offers sacrifices on it. He also writes a copy of the law on stones as a lasting public record.

parts.label: The law read to all (vv. 33-35)
parts.note: Half the people stand before Mount Gerizim and half before Mount Ebal, with the ark (the sacred chest that stood for God's presence) between them, to hear the blessings for keeping the covenant and the curses for breaking it. The text stresses that everyone heard, including women, children and foreigners living among them.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand the destruction of a whole city that the text says God commanded: some read it as literal history, others as ancient war language that exaggerates, and others as a story to be read through the later teaching of Jesus.
think: This chapter moves straight from the slaughter of a city to a solemn gathering where everyone hears the law read; what do you make of the way people throughout history have tied victory in war to their sense of the sacred?
